title: Musk Confirms TSMC Talks for a Texas 'Terafab' as Rare-Earth Deadline Looms
subhead: Elon Musk says SpaceX is in talks with TSMC about a Texas chip complex, while China's November 10 rare-earth export controls edge closer and a Gotion-VW battery deal reshapes Spain's EV value chain.

sections.heading: TSMC and Musk Explore a Texas 'Terafab'
sections.body:
Elon Musk confirmed on X that SpaceX is in discussions with TSMC about collaborating on his planned 'Terafab' chip complex, saying: 'Just discussions, but something may come of it.' The confirmation follows reporting from the Commercial Times and analyst Tim Culpan's Culpium newsletter that TSMC is exploring a partnership that could include a new fab in Texas, according to TrendForce.

Several structures are reportedly on the table. Under one, TSMC would own and operate the fab while SpaceX and Terafab take equity stakes, commit to wafer purchases, or both. Under another, SpaceX and Terafab would hold majority ownership while TSMC contributes less capital but provides process technology and operating expertise. Taiwan's Business Today notes the talks may reflect setbacks in Musk's earlier attempts to work with Intel and Samsung, and that Terafab's push for vertically integrated manufacturing clashes with TSMC's pure-play foundry model built around fabless customers such as Nvidia, Apple, AMD and Broadcom.

The talks land alongside TSMC's wider US expansion. Market reports cited by Taiwan's Central News Agency suggest TSMC is weighing a second US hub near Dallas, Texas, potentially involving six more advanced fabs, on top of the roughly $100 billion it has committed to Arizona — bringing planned investment in that state to about $265 billion. TSMC has already raised its 2026 capex guidance to $60-64 billion and says spending over the next three years will significantly exceed the prior three-year period.
sections.whyItMatters: If it proceeds, a Terafab tied to TSMC would fuse two of the most strategic US industrial programs — leading-edge logic and Musk's vertically integrated AI/space stack — into one Texas footprint. It also tests whether TSMC's pure-play model can absorb an anchor customer that wants to own the factory.

sections.heading: China's November 10 Rare-Earth Deadline Approaches
sections.body:
Rare-earth market participants are focused on 10 November 2026, when China's expanded export controls are due to be reintroduced unless the current suspension is extended, according to Fastmarkets. Under China's Announcement No. 61, licensing requirements can apply to foreign-made products containing specified Chinese-origin rare-earth materials above certain thresholds, products made using covered Chinese technologies, or products incorporating Chinese-origin controlled items — carrying controls deeper into global supply chains, including equipment and technology for rare-earth separation, strip-alloy production and magnet manufacturing.

China's April 2025 heavy rare-earth controls already widened a price gap between Chinese and ex-China markets. Fastmarkets data shows dysprosium oxide in Europe trading at about 4.9 times the domestic Chinese price, and terbium oxide at 3.8 times. Chinese customs data shows no dysprosium or terbium oxide exported to Japan — the largest consumer outside China — in 2026.

The response is accelerating but incomplete. G7 members agreed in June to cut reliance on any single rare-earth and magnet supplier to below 60% by 2030, and governments have committed hundreds of millions of dollars since April 2025, including a $1.6 billion US award to USA Rare Earth and a $550 million package for MP Materials. Yet recyclers remain dependent on Chinese equipment and extractants: Mkango's managing director Nielson Beddoe told Fastmarkets that purpose-built Chinese equipment can cost roughly one-third of Western alternatives.
sections.whyItMatters: The November deadline is now the key test of whether the US-China minerals truce holds. If the suspension lapses, licensing would reach into finished products worldwide — not just raw ore — raising costs for magnets used in EVs, wind turbines and defense systems.

sections.heading: Gotion Takes 49% of VW's Spain Battery Plant
sections.body:
Volkswagen Group, its battery unit PowerCo and China's Gotion High-Tech announced on September 28 that Gotion will invest about 1.1 billion euros ($1.29 billion) for a 49% stake in PowerCo's battery-cell plant in Sagunto, eastern Spain, with PowerCo retaining 51% and operations intended to start in 2027, according to Global Times. The first phase is now planned at up to 30 GWh of annual capacity — 50% above the 20 GWh initially considered — to produce LFP-based Unified Cells for VW's Spanish EV production.

The deal sits within a broader push. Stellantis and China's CATL are investing up to 4.1 billion euros ($4.62 billion) in a 50-50 joint venture for an LFP plant in Zaragoza, with production scheduled to start by the end of 2026. Chery has partnered with Spain's Ebro to revive production at Nissan's former Barcelona plant, and Ford and Geely agreed to a joint venture around the Almussafes plant in Valencia. Spain builds more than 2 million vehicles a year as Europe's second-largest vehicle producer, but much of its industry sits inside multinational groups — a vulnerability highlighted by VW's consideration of phasing out the SEAT brand after 2030.
sections.whyItMatters: Europe still lacks large-scale LFP battery capacity, and this shows the emerging template: Chinese partners supply the battery technology and capital while European plants supply the factories and market access. It keeps Spanish assembly lines running even as Chinese firms move further upstream into cathode production and recycling.

sections.heading: Starship Reaches Orbit With First Starlink V3 Payload
sections.body:
SpaceX's Starship Flight 14 reached orbit on its first orbital attempt on September 28 and deployed 26 Starlink V3 operational satellites, which Musk said were 'operating nominally,' according to AOL/247 Wall St. Musk called it the 'first orbital flight of Starship successful.' SpaceX describes the V3 satellite as roughly an order of magnitude more capable than V2.

The commercial stakes are concrete. Connectivity revenue reached $4.29 billion in Q2 2026, up 66% year over year, with Enterprise and Government up 108%, per SpaceX's SEC filings. Starlink has over 12 million subscribers, though ARPU slipped from $85 to $66 as cheaper plans pulled in new users. Management says a meaningful service upgrade requires about 1,000 V3 satellites, a threshold it expects around Q2 2027. Still unproven: catching and rapidly re-flying the ship. Musk has said SpaceX would attempt a tower catch of the ship on the next flight, subject to regulatory approval. Quarterly capex hit $18.37 billion, with $15.83 billion going to AI compute.
sections.whyItMatters: An orbital Starship carrying working V3 satellites turns the vehicle into a delivery system for Starlink's next capacity jump — and gives SpaceX a near-monopoly-class launch asset for commercial and government constellations. The unproven piece is reusability economics: a successful ship catch before year-end would validate the cost model behind the V3 buildout.

sections.heading: Germany's Huawei Position Erodes as Regulator Signals RAN Is 'Critical'
sections.body:
Germany's Federal Network Agency has proposed reclassifying the 5G radio access network as a critical element, in a little-noticed filing with the European Commission picked up by WirtschaftsWoche and reported by Light Reading. The draft states that 'all functions of the gNodeB are to be classified as a critical function.' The change would undercut the legal foundation German operators have used to justify keeping Huawei gear: Deutsche Telekom CEO Timotheus Höttges had previously argued the RAN was not a critical element under German law.

Chinese vendors currently serve about a third of European business, per Assembly Research. Analyst firm Strand Consult estimates Huawei accounts for about 58% of Germany's RAN footprint, around 46,000 sites, and puts a full swap-out at roughly 2.5 billion euros ($2.8 billion) — about 5% of the operators' collective annual revenue. Huawei has resisted such reclassifications before, telling Finland's regulator last year that 'the gNB does not control traffic, manage connections or user profiles.' The agency said one of four manufacturers is clearly against expanding the list of critical functions while the other three support it.
sections.whyItMatters: Classifying the RAN as critical would make it much harder for Berlin to avoid a ban and removes the legal cover operators have relied on. It is a regulatory step, not a ban — but it narrows the political space to keep Huawei in Germany's networks.

sections.heading: US and China Trade Cyber Allegations
sections.body:
Beijing rejected a US accusation of state-sponsored hacking and accused Washington of double standards, after the US Justice Department and FBI seized domains associated with QScan and QTRouter, two platforms allegedly operated by a China state-sponsored group the US calls QTFY, according to Outlook India and Anadolu Agency. US court documents allege QTFY was employed by Nanjing Xinjiuwei Network Technology and provided hacking services to customers including China's Ministry of State Security and the People's Liberation Army. Victims named in the US statement include NASA, the Federal Reserve, the Department of Energy and the US Senate.

Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Lin Jian said Beijing 'firmly rejects' the accusation and 'will not accept any vilification in the name of so-called cybersecurity issues,' pointing to China's own previously disclosed allegation of an NSA cyberattack on its National Time Service Center. Lin called on the two countries to manage cyber risk through 'equal-footed dialogue and consultation.'
sections.whyItMatters: Both governments are publicly trading breach claims while pushing for stabilization elsewhere. The dispute reflects how cyber operations remain one of the least de-escalated arenas in the relationship — even as trade and chip policy show signs of a truce.

bottomLine: Today's developments show the two tracks of the US-China tech relationship running in opposite directions. On the commercial track, a possible TSMC-Musk Texas fab and Chinese battery investment in Spain point to deepening integration of capital and capacity. On the strategic track, China's November 10 rare-earth deadline and the mutual cyber breach accusations show the coercive instruments remain loaded. TSMC's Texas expansion is the clearest signal: leading-edge manufacturing is being pulled toward the US by both policy and anchor-customer demand, while Europe's battery buildout increasingly depends on the Chinese partners it is also trying to contain.
sources: TrendForce, Commercial Times, Culpium (Tim Culpan), Central News Agency (Taiwan), Business Today (Taiwan), Fastmarkets, Global Times, Reuters, AOL/247 Wall St, SpaceX SEC filings, Light Reading, WirtschaftsWoche, Assembly Research, Strand Consult, Outlook India, Anadolu Agency, TRT World, Bloomberg News
